lead.en: An India-bound fleet drifts west and claims a new land

summary.en: Pedro Álvares Cabral's Portuguese fleet, bound for India, swung far to the west and reached the coast of Brazil. Cabral claimed the land for Portugal, beginning the colonisation of South America's largest country.

title.en: The Moriori settle the Chatham Islands

lead.en: Polynesians settle the Chathams and renounce war

summary.en: Around 1500 descendants of the first Māori moved to the harsh Chatham Islands, 800 km from New Zealand. There they became the Moriori; by their tradition the chief Nunuku-whenua forbade killing, and disputes were settled by fights to first blood. In 1835 Māori from the North Island invaded and enslaved the Moriori.

lead.en: Shah Ismail makes Shia Islam the faith of all Iran

summary.en: Ismail I was proclaimed shah in Tabriz and made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion. The Safavid state reunified Iran and for two centuries was the Ottoman Empire's chief rival in the east.

title.en: The Badaling section of the Great Wall

lead.en: The most-visited stretch of the Wall is younger than the Kremlin

summary.en: The wall at Badaling pass was built under the Ming in the early 16th century to guard the approaches to Beijing. It was the first section restored and opened to visitors, in 1957, and hundreds of millions of people and many heads of state have walked it since.

lead.en: Michelangelo paints the summit of the High Renaissance

summary.en: Commissioned by Pope Julius II, Michelangelo spent four years painting the chapel's vault with scenes from Genesis. The frescoes, including the Creation of Adam, became a summit of High Renaissance art.

title.en: Afonso I becomes King of Kongo

lead.en: A Catholic king binds Kongo to Portugal

summary.en: The Christian ruler Afonso I took the throne of Kongo after defeating his brother. He promoted Catholicism and ties with Portugal, yet in letters to the Portuguese king protested the ravages of the slave trade.

lead.en: Portugal seizes the key to the spice trade

summary.en: Afonso de Albuquerque's fleet seized Malacca, the greatest trading port of Southeast Asia. Portugal gained control of the Strait of Malacca and a key to the spice trade between the Indian Ocean and China.

lead.en: Ottoman cannon defeat Shah Ismail's army

summary.en: Ottoman sultan Selim I crushed Shah Ismail I's army thanks to artillery and musket-armed janissaries. The Ottomans took eastern Anatolia, and the Sunni–Shia rivalry of the two empires shaped the region for generations.

lead.en: A white elephant from India becomes the darling of Rome

summary.en: In 1514 King Manuel I of Portugal gave Pope Leo X a white Indian elephant. Hanno danced for crowds, sprayed onlookers with water and joined processions; when he died two years later, the pope wrote his epitaph and Raphael reportedly designed a memorial fresco.

lead.en: The most famous rhino, drawn by an artist who never saw one

summary.en: In 1515 a live rhinoceros from India reached Lisbon, the first seen in Europe since Roman times. Albrecht Dürer made his woodcut from a sketch and a letter, adding armour plates and a horn on the back — and Europeans pictured rhinos that way for over two centuries.

lead.en: A protest against indulgences sparks the Reformation

summary.en: Monk and professor Martin Luther issued 95 theses attacking the sale of indulgences. Spread rapidly by the printing press, they launched the Reformation, which split Western Christianity.

title.en: Battle of Ridaniya and conquest of Egypt

lead.en: The Ottomans take Egypt and the holy cities of Arabia

summary.en: Near Cairo, Selim I's army defeated the Mamluks of Sultan Tuman Bay. Egypt became Ottoman, along with guardianship of Mecca and Medina, strengthening Ottoman claims to leadership of the Islamic world.

lead.en: The Victoria becomes the first ship to sail around the world

summary.en: Ferdinand Magellan's Spanish expedition found a strait at the tip of South America and crossed the Pacific. Magellan was killed in the Philippines; the Victoria under Elcano completed the first circumnavigation in 1522.

lead.en: Ottoman power peaks, from Mohács to the gates of Vienna

summary.en: Under Sultan Suleiman I the Ottoman Empire reached its zenith, taking Belgrade and Rhodes, crushing Hungary at Mohács and besieging Vienna. At home he was called Kanuni, 'the Lawgiver', for codifying the empire's laws.

title.en: The Portuguese seek Prester John in Ethiopia

lead.en: Europe finally reaches the realm of legendary Prester John

summary.en: For centuries Europeans believed in a distant Christian kingdom of Prester John who would help them against the Muslims. In 1520 a Portuguese embassy landed at Massawa and spent six years at the court of Emperor Lebna Dengel; its chaplain Francisco Álvares described Ethiopia as Prester John's land.

lead.en: The Aztec empire ends and Mexico City rises from its ruins

summary.en: After a long siege, Hernán Cortés's Spaniards and their Tlaxcalan allies took the Aztec capital, already ravaged by smallpox. The Aztec Empire fell, and Mexico City, capital of New Spain, rose on its ruins.

lead.en: The largest forced migration in history

place.en: Luanda (Angola), the largest port of embarkation

summary.en: The first slave ship known to sail directly from Africa to the Americas left around 1526; the last reached Cuba in 1867. In between, European and American traders embarked some 12.5 million Africans, of whom about 10.7 million survived the crossing. Most were taken to Brazil and the Caribbean, about 400,000 to North America.

lead.en: Babur's guns found the Mughal Empire

summary.en: Babur, ruler of Kabul, used cannon and muskets to rout the army of Delhi sultan Ibrahim Lodi. The victory founded the Mughal Empire, which ruled most of the Indian subcontinent for over two centuries.

lead.en: Hungary's king falls and his realm is carved into three

summary.en: On 29 August 1526 Suleiman the Magnificent's Ottoman army crushed the Hungarian forces. King Louis II died, and Hungary was soon divided between the Habsburgs, the Ottoman Empire and Transylvania.

lead.en: Christian Ethiopia nearly falls; Portuguese muskets save it

summary.en: In 1529 Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim of the Adal Sultanate, nicknamed Gragn, 'the Left-handed', crushed Emperor Lebna Dengel at Shimbra Kure. Within a decade his forces overran most of Ethiopia and burned many churches and monasteries. Help came from 400 Portuguese musketeers under Cristóvão da Gama, son of Vasco; in 1543 Ahmad was killed at the Battle of Wayna Daga.

title.en: Apparition of Our Lady of Guadalupe

lead.en: The shrine that became a symbol of Mexico

summary.en: According to tradition, in December 1531 the Virgin Mary, dark-skinned, appeared to the baptised Indigenous man Juan Diego on Tepeyac hill, and her image was miraculously imprinted on his cloak, or tilma. Her cult fused Catholicism with local tradition. The 1810 independence revolt marched under her banner, and her basilica in Mexico City is one of the most visited shrines in the world.

lead.en: A small band of Spaniards captures the Inca ruler

summary.en: Francisco Pizarro's band of fewer than 200 men captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa. After receiving a huge gold ransom the Spaniards executed him in 1533, and the Inca Empire, split by civil war, soon collapsed.

lead.en: The king heads the Church himself — Anglicanism is born

summary.en: Denied a papal annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, Henry VIII passed the Act of Supremacy in 1534 and became head of the Church of England. The dissolution of the monasteries and seizure of their lands followed.

lead.en: Tales of warrior women named the world's greatest river

summary.en: In late 1541 Francisco de Orellana's party split from Gonzalo Pizarro's expedition to look for food and could not return against the current. Over eight months the Spaniards drifted to the Atlantic, reaching it in August 1542, the first Europeans to do so. Chronicler Gaspar de Carvajal described battles with warrior women, and the river was named after the Amazons of Greek myth.

lead.en: The Sun at the centre — the scientific revolution begins

summary.en: Nicolaus Copernicus's On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, printed in Nuremberg, put the Sun rather than the Earth at the centre. Published in the year of his death, it began the Scientific Revolution.

lead.en: An anatomist corrects Galen, who had dissected apes

summary.en: Andreas Vesalius did his own dissections and showed that Galen had described human anatomy from apes and pigs, with hundreds of errors doctors had repeated for over a thousand years. The book came out in 1543, the same year as Copernicus's.

lead.en: A mystery fever wipes out much of Mexico's native population

summary.en: A mysterious hemorrhagic fever the Aztecs called cocoliztli killed an estimated 5 to 15 million people, a large share of Mexico's native population. Its cause is still debated; one hypothesis is paratyphoid fever. That same year, the Council of Trent opened in Europe.

lead.en: Andean silver reshapes the world economy

summary.en: Vast silver deposits were found in the Cerro Rico in the Andes. Potosí became one of the world's largest cities, and silver mined by indigenous forced labour (the mita) flowed to Europe and China, transforming the world economy.

lead.en: A grand prince takes the title of tsar for the first time

summary.en: On 16 January 1547 Grand Prince Ivan IV was crowned in the Kremlin's Dormition Cathedral, the first to take the title of tsar. This created the Tsardom of Russia, which lasted until the empire was proclaimed in 1721.

lead.en: Sinan's masterpiece crowns the Ottoman golden age

summary.en: Architect Mimar Sinan built this mosque complex, with schools, a hospital and baths, for Suleiman the Magnificent. It became a symbol of the golden age of the Ottoman Empire, then at the height of its power.

lead.en: Ivan IV annexes the khanate and gains the Volga

summary.en: Ivan IV's army stormed Kazan and annexed the Kazan Khanate to Muscovy. Russia gained the Volga and a road to the east; St Basil's Cathedral in Moscow was built to commemorate the victory.

lead.en: Nine churches in one, built to mark the fall of Kazan

summary.en: The Cathedral of the Intercession on Red Square was built in 1555–1561 on Ivan the Terrible's orders to celebrate the capture of Kazan. It later took the name of the holy fool Basil, who was buried beside it.

lead.en: Loess cave homes collapse in history's deadliest disaster

summary.en: On 23 January 1556 an earthquake in the Wei River valley killed an estimated 830,000 people, the deadliest on record. Many lived in yaodong cave dwellings cut into loess cliffs, which collapsed. The same year, Ivan the Terrible annexed Astrakhan.

title.en: Akbar and the Second Battle of Panipat

lead.en: A 13-year-old ruler wins back northern India for the Mughals

summary.en: The army of the 13-year-old Akbar defeated the general Hemu and restored Mughal rule in northern India. Akbar reigned for nearly half a century, united most of the subcontinent and pursued religious tolerance.

lead.en: The first precisely dated Russian printed book

summary.en: On 1 March 1564 Ivan Fyodorov and Pyotr Mstislavets finished printing the Apostol, the first precisely dated book printed in Russia. Fyodorov later worked in Lviv and Ostroh, where he printed the Ostrog Bible.

lead.en: Ivan the Terrible's private domain of executions and seizures

summary.en: In 1565 Ivan the Terrible set aside part of the country as the oprichnina under his personal rule, with its own guard. The oprichniki carried out mass executions and confiscations, culminating in the sack of Novgorod in 1570. It was abolished in 1572.

lead.en: One battle, and the splendid city of Vijayanagara lies in ruins

summary.en: In January 1565 a coalition of the Deccan sultanates crushed the army of the Vijayanagara Empire, the last great Hindu power of southern India. The regent Rama Raya was captured and beheaded. For months the victors looted and burned the capital, one of the largest cities in the world at the time; its ruins at Hampi are now a UNESCO site.

lead.en: Spaniards sought Solomon's gold and named the islands for it

summary.en: Álvaro de Mendaña's expedition sailed from Callao in search of the fabled southern continent and in February 1568 reached Santa Isabel. The Spaniards spent six months exploring the archipelago, clashed with islanders over food and returned empty-handed, but rumours of riches gave the islands the name of Solomon. Mendaña's second voyage, in 1595, ended with his death on Santa Cruz.

lead.en: Poland and Lithuania merge into a single Commonwealth

summary.en: On 1 July 1569 the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania merged into the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth with a jointly elected king and Sejm. Ukrainian lands passed from Lithuania to the Polish Crown.

lead.en: The Holy League halts Ottoman expansion at sea

summary.en: The fleet of the Holy League — Spain, Venice and the Papacy — destroyed the Ottoman fleet off Greece. The greatest galley battle checked Ottoman expansion in the Mediterranean; Cervantes was wounded in it.

title.en: Spanish Manila and the Manila galleons

lead.en: Silver for silk: the first regular link of Asia and America

summary.en: Miguel López de Legazpi founded Spanish Manila. Galleons sailing between Manila and Acapulco carried American silver in exchange for Chinese silk and porcelain, linking Asia and the Americas by regular trade for the first time.

lead.en: A Paris royal wedding turns into a massacre of Protestants

summary.en: On the night of 24 August 1572, days after the wedding of Henry of Navarre and Margaret of Valois, Catholics began killing the Huguenots gathered in Paris. The massacre spread to other cities and claimed thousands of lives.

lead.en: A new star beyond the Moon shatters the idea of fixed heavens

summary.en: In November 1572 a new star brighter than Venus blazed in Cassiopeia. Tycho Brahe showed it lay far beyond the Moon, undermining the belief in unchanging heavens. The same year saw the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre in France and the Battle of Molodi near Moscow.

lead.en: A king gives an astronomer an entire island to observe from

summary.en: King Frederick II of Denmark granted Tycho Brahe the island of Hven, where he built a castle-observatory with its own printing press and paper mill. Without a telescope, he gathered the most precise observations of his age, which Kepler used to find his laws of planetary motion.

lead.en: King Sebastian falls, and Portugal loses its independence

summary.en: Moroccan forces destroyed the army of King Sebastian I of Portugal, who died in battle along with two Moroccan claimants. Morocco rose under Ahmad al-Mansur, while Portugal passed to the Spanish king in 1580.

title.en: Yasuke, the African retainer of Nobunaga

lead.en: An African man becomes a retainer of Japan's great warlord

summary.en: In 1581 Jesuits brought an African attendant to Kyoto, where crowds rushed to see him. Oda Nobunaga reportedly had his skin scrubbed, thinking it was ink, then took him into service with a stipend and a sword. A year later Yasuke was with Nobunaga when he died at Honnō-ji.

lead.en: Ten days vanish from the calendar most of the world now uses

summary.en: In 1582 Pope Gregory XIII introduced a new calendar: Thursday 4 October was followed directly by Friday 15 October. Protestant countries adopted it gradually, and Russia only in 1918.

lead.en: Cossacks defeat Kuchum, opening Russia's road to the Pacific

summary.en: Yermak's Cossack band defeated Khan Kuchum and took his capital Isker. This began Russia's annexation of Siberia; by 1639 Russian explorers had reached the Pacific Ocean.

lead.en: The first Russian town in Siberia

summary.en: A few years after Yermak's campaign, the voivodes Vasily Sukin and Ivan Myasnoy built a fort on the Tura river by the old Tatar town of Chingi-Tura. Tyumen became the first Russian town in Siberia and the gateway for the push further east.

lead.en: The giant gun that, despite the jokes, was fired

summary.en: Master founder Andrey Chokhov cast the roughly 39-tonne Tsar Cannon in 1586. It is famous as a gun that never fired, but specialists from the Artillery Academy found powder residue in its barrel during a 1980 inspection.

lead.en: An English colony vanishes, leaving one word carved on a post

summary.en: In 1587 more than a hundred colonists settled on Roanoke Island, where Virginia Dare became the first English child born in the Americas. Governor John White sailed home for supplies, but war with Spain delayed him until 1590. He found the site deserted, with CROATOAN carved on a post.

lead.en: England repels invasion and turns toward sea power

summary.en: Philip II sent a great fleet to invade England. After the battle off Gravelines and storms on the voyage home the Armada lost many ships; England kept its independence and Protestantism and began its rise as a sea power.

lead.en: The Russian Church gains rank equal to the Eastern patriarchates

summary.en: In January 1589, with Patriarch Jeremias II of Constantinople taking part, Metropolitan Job was installed as the first Patriarch of Moscow. The Russian Church gained a rank equal to the eastern patriarchates.

title.en: Battle of Tondibi and fall of Songhai

lead.en: Moroccan muskets topple West Africa's largest empire

summary.en: A Moroccan army under Judar Pasha crossed the Sahara with firearms and defeated Askia Ishaq II. The Songhai Empire, West Africa's largest state, collapsed, and Gao and Timbuktu lost their former importance.

lead.en: Korea and Ming China hold back a Japanese invasion

summary.en: Toyotomi Hideyoshi's armies landed at Busan and invaded Korea, aiming to conquer China. Joseon, aided by Ming China and Admiral Yi Sun-sin's fleet, held out; the Japanese withdrew after Hideyoshi's death, leaving Korea devastated.

lead.en: Elizabeth I’s godson invents a flushing toilet

summary.en: The courtier-poet John Harington built a flushing toilet with a cistern at his house and described it in his 1596 satire The Metamorphosis of Ajax. The title was a pun on “jakes”, slang for a privy.

lead.en: Famine, pretenders and invasion — until the Romanovs are chosen

summary.en: After the Rurikid dynasty died out, Russia was engulfed by famine, pretenders, civil war and Polish and Swedish intervention. Minin and Pozharsky's militia freed Moscow in 1612, and in 1613 an assembly elected Michael Romanov tsar.

lead.en: Henry IV grants Huguenots freedom of worship, ending the wars

summary.en: King Henry IV, himself a former Huguenot, signed the edict in 1598, granting Protestants freedom of worship and civil rights. It ended decades of religious war in France and stood until its revocation in 1685.

lead.en: Shah Abbas turns Isfahan into 'half the world'

summary.en: Shah Abbas I moved the Safavid capital to Isfahan and surrounded the vast Naqsh-e Jahan Square with palaces, mosques and a bazaar. The city became one of the world's most splendid — 'Isfahan is half the world', Persians said.

lead.en: Tokugawa's victory brings Japan two and a half centuries of peace

summary.en: Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated a coalition of western daimyo and became Japan's de facto ruler. Named shogun in 1603, he founded the Tokugawa shogunate, based in Edo, which kept Japan at peace for two and a half centuries.

lead.en: Peruvian ash chills the north and likely brings famine to Russia

summary.en: In February 1600 Huaynaputina produced the largest recorded eruption in South American history. Its stratospheric ash cooled the Northern Hemisphere, and researchers see a probable link to the Russian famine of 1601–1603 under Boris Godunov, a prelude to the Time of Troubles.

lead.en: A trading company that would come to rule India

summary.en: On 31 December 1600 Elizabeth I granted London merchants a monopoly on trade with Asia. The East India Company began with pepper and textiles and by the mid-19th century ruled most of India with its own army. After the Indian Rebellion of 1857 its territories passed to the British Crown.

title.en: The burial of Chief Roi Mata

lead.en: A Vanuatu legend confirmed by excavation

summary.en: According to tradition, around 1600 Chief Roi Mata made peace among the warring clans of central Vanuatu and on his death was buried on the islet of Artok with dozens of his followers. In 1967 the French archaeologist José Garanger excavated a mass burial of about 50 people there, matching the oral account. In 2008 Chief Roi Mata's Domain became Vanuatu's first UNESCO World Heritage Site.

lead.en: A Jesuit draws a world map for China with China at the centre

summary.en: In 1602 in Beijing the Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci and Chinese scholars printed a large map of the world. To please his hosts he put the Pacific in the middle, leaving China near the centre. For many Chinese it was their first sight of the Americas.

lead.en: All-male kabuki was invented by a woman

summary.en: Around 1603 the dancer Okuni began performing bold sketches on the dry bed of the Kamo River in Kyoto, playing male roles herself. Kabuki was born. But in 1629 the shogunate banned women from the stage, and ever since, all kabuki roles have been played by men.

lead.en: The last galactic star blast seen with the naked eye

summary.en: In October 1604 a supernova flared in Ophiuchus, and Johannes Kepler followed it from Prague for over a year. It remains the last supernova in our galaxy seen with the naked eye. In the same weeks, False Dmitry I crossed into Russia.

lead.en: For nearly a century runaway slaves fought off colonial armies

summary.en: Around 1605, slaves fleeing sugar plantations founded the free settlement of Palmares in the forested hills of northeastern Brazil. By various estimates it eventually held more than ten thousand people. The quilombo repelled dozens of Portuguese and Dutch expeditions and fell only in 1694. Its last leader, Zumbi, was killed on 20 November 1695, now celebrated in Brazil as Black Consciousness Day.

lead.en: A parody of chivalry becomes the first modern novel

summary.en: The first part of Miguel de Cervantes's novel about the knight of La Mancha appeared in Madrid; the second followed in 1615. A parody of chivalric romances, it is often called the first modern novel.

lead.en: The first Europeans in Australia took it for New Guinea

summary.en: In 1606 the Dutch ship Duyfken under Willem Janszoon, searching for gold and spices south of New Guinea, sailed along the west coast of Cape York. It is the first documented European landing in Australia. The encounter with Aboriginal people ended in a clash, and Janszoon judged the coast swampy and barren, assuming it was part of New Guinea.

lead.en: England's first permanent foothold in North America

summary.en: Settlers of the Virginia Company founded Jamestown, the first permanent English settlement in North America. Tobacco made the colony viable; in 1619 the first enslaved Africans were brought there.

lead.en: The birth of New France and French-speaking Canada

summary.en: On 3 July 1608 Samuel de Champlain founded a fortified fur-trading post on the St. Lawrence River. Only 8 of the 28 settlers survived the first winter. Quebec became the capital of New France, which stretched to the Great Lakes and the Mississippi. It is one of North America's oldest cities, and French has been spoken there for more than four centuries.

lead.en: Mission towns where natives armed against slave raiders

summary.en: In 1609 the Jesuits founded their first reduction, or mission town, among the Guaraní. Soon there were about thirty such towns, with a population exceeding 100,000 by the 1730s. They built Baroque churches, printed books in Guaraní and kept their own militia against Brazilian slave raiders. In 1767 the Spanish crown expelled the Jesuits, and the reductions declined.

lead.en: Moons of Jupiter and lunar mountains back Copernicus

summary.en: In The Starry Messenger, Galileo Galilei described mountains on the Moon, countless new stars and four moons of Jupiter seen through his telescope. The observations became powerful evidence for the Copernican system.

lead.en: A people's militia drives the Polish garrison out of the Kremlin

summary.en: At the end of the Time of Troubles, the militia of Kuzma Minin and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky repulsed Hetman Chodkiewicz's relief army in September 1612 and that autumn forced the Polish–Lithuanian garrison in the Kremlin to surrender.

title.en: Election of Michael Romanov as Tsar

lead.en: An assembly ends the Time of Troubles and founds a dynasty

summary.en: On 3 March 1613 the Zemsky Sobor elected 16-year-old Michael Romanov as tsar. This ended the Time of Troubles and founded the Romanov dynasty, which ruled Russia until 1917.

lead.en: Japanese samurai cross two oceans to reach Rome

summary.en: An embassy sent by the daimyo Date Masamune under Hasekura Tsunenaga crossed via Mexico to Spain in 1614 and met Pope Paul V in Rome in 1615. Some of the Japanese stayed in Coria del Río near Seville, where hundreds of people today bear the surname Japón.

lead.en: A Dutch captain nails a pewter plate to a post in Australia

summary.en: In October 1616 Captain Dirk Hartog landed in Western Australia and nailed a pewter plate recording his visit to a post. Eighty-one years later Willem de Vlamingh found it, left a copy and took the original to Amsterdam. It is the oldest surviving European artefact from Australia.

lead.en: A religious conflict ends in a system of sovereign states

summary.en: Beginning with the Defenestration of Prague as a Protestant–Catholic conflict within the Holy Roman Empire, the war drew in almost every European power. Germany lost perhaps a third of its population; the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 founded the modern system of sovereign states.

lead.en: Officials are thrown from a castle window — and survive

summary.en: Bohemian Protestant nobles threw two royal regents and their secretary out of a window of Prague Castle. All three survived: Catholics credited the Virgin Mary, Protestants a dung heap below. The incident sparked the Thirty Years' War.

lead.en: The Dutch gain their spice-trade capital in Asia

summary.en: Jan Pieterszoon Coen seized Jayakarta and founded Batavia on its site as the Asian headquarters of the Dutch East India Company. From here the Dutch ran the spice trade and their colonial empire in Indonesia.

lead.en: The Pilgrims signed a self-government pact on board

summary.en: In November 1620 the Mayflower brought 102 passengers, among them English Puritan Separatists, to the shores of New England. While still aboard, the men signed the Mayflower Compact on self-government. Half the colonists died in the first winter; the Wampanoag helped the rest survive. Their shared harvest feast of 1621 is traditionally seen as the first Thanksgiving.

lead.en: The end of Portuguese dominance in the Persian Gulf

summary.en: From 1515 the Portuguese held a fortress on the island of Hormuz and controlled the trade of the Persian Gulf. In 1622 the forces of Shah Abbas I, backed by ships of the English East India Company, took the island after a two-month siege. Trade moved to a new mainland port, Bandar Abbas, and the English and Dutch began to push the Portuguese aside in the Indian Ocean.

lead.en: For forty years she outfought and outwitted the Portuguese

summary.en: In 1622 Nzinga negotiated with the Portuguese governor in Luanda; legend says that when no chair was offered, a servant knelt to become her seat. In 1624 Nzinga became ruler of Ndongo. Driven out by the Portuguese, she conquered the kingdom of Matamba, allied with the Dutch and fought on almost until her death in 1663. Today she is a national heroine of Angola.

lead.en: Cattle's wild ancestor vanishes despite royal protection

summary.en: In 1627 the last known aurochs, a cow, died in the royal forest at Jaktorów. Polish kings had protected the herd of these wild ancestors of cattle for centuries, but not from disease and poaching. Meanwhile, the Thirty Years' War raged across Europe.

lead.en: Sweden's mighty warship sinks less than a mile out

summary.en: On 10 August 1628 Gustavus Adolphus's newest warship set off on her maiden voyage, keeled over in a gust after about 1,300 metres and sank in the harbour. Raised almost intact in 1961, the Vasa now fills one of Scandinavia's most visited museums.

lead.en: A tomb for a beloved wife becomes the Mughal masterpiece

summary.en: Mughal emperor Shah Jahan began building a white marble mausoleum in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Built by thousands of craftsmen, the Taj Mahal became the masterpiece of Mughal architecture.

lead.en: Legend says a man flew on wings from Europe to Asia

summary.en: The traveller Evliya Çelebi wrote that the scholar Hezârfen Ahmed Çelebi leapt from Galata Tower on artificial wings and glided across the Bosphorus to Üsküdar. Sultan Murad IV rewarded him, then exiled him as too dangerous. No other source confirms the story.

lead.en: 'And yet it moves' first appears in print 120 years later

summary.en: In 1633 the Inquisition condemned Galileo for defending Copernicus, and he publicly recanted. The defiant 'And yet it moves!' he supposedly muttered first appeared in print only in 1757.

lead.en: A Mughal throne that cost more than the Taj Mahal

summary.en: In 1635 Shah Jahan first sat on a throne that jewellers had worked on for seven years: gold, rubies, emeralds and pearls, crowned with peacocks. It reportedly cost twice as much as the Taj Mahal. Nader Shah carried it off to Iran in 1739, and it later vanished.

lead.en: Emperor Fasilides gives Ethiopia a permanent capital

summary.en: Emperor Fasilides made Gondar Ethiopia's permanent capital and built a stone castle there. The royal enclosure of Fasil Ghebbi, with its palaces and churches, became the centre of Ethiopian culture for two centuries.

lead.en: A college in a colony only six years old

summary.en: In 1636 the legislature of the Massachusetts Bay Colony voted money for a college, the first in English America. It was named after the clergyman John Harvard, who left it his library and half his estate.

lead.en: A Gold Coast fortress becomes a hub of the slave trade

summary.en: The Dutch West India Company took the castle of São Jorge da Mina on the Gold Coast from the Portuguese. Elmina became a major hub of the Atlantic slave trade; many thousands of Africans passed through its dungeons.

lead.en: A single tulip bulb costs more than a decade of wages

summary.en: In the winter of 1636–37 the Dutch traded tulip bulbs still in the ground through contracts signed in taverns, and prices for rare varieties soared. In February 1637 the market collapsed within days — though modern historians doubt it ruined many people.

lead.en: A border drawn in 1639 that still largely holds today

summary.en: The peace between the Ottoman Empire and Safavid Iran ended the war of 1623–1639. Baghdad and Mesopotamia, retaken by Sultan Murad IV a year earlier, stayed Ottoman, while the Caucasus was divided. The Zuhab line roughly matches Iran's present-day borders with Turkey and Iraq.

lead.en: A tiny island becomes Japan's only window to the West

summary.en: Having expelled the Portuguese and banned Christianity, the shogunate confined the Dutch trading post to the artificial island of Dejima. For over two centuries it was nearly Japan's only window on the Western world.

lead.en: Southern lands appear on European maps for the first time

summary.en: Dutch navigator Abel Tasman became the first European to reach Tasmania and the west coast of New Zealand. A clash with Māori in Golden Bay prevented a landing, but these southern lands first appeared on European maps.

lead.en: A king is executed and England briefly becomes a republic

summary.en: Charles I's conflict with Parliament turned into war between Cavaliers and Roundheads. Oliver Cromwell's New Model Army won, the king was executed and England briefly became a republic.

title.en: Fall of the Ming, rise of the Qing

lead.en: The Manchus enter Beijing, founding China's last dynasty

summary.en: Li Zicheng's rebels took Beijing and the last Ming emperor, Chongzhen, hanged himself. General Wu Sangui let the Manchus through Shanhai Pass; they seized the capital and founded the Qing dynasty, which ruled China until 1912.

lead.en: A coin weighing almost 20 kilograms

summary.en: Copper-rich Sweden began issuing money in 1644 as rectangular copper plates worth their weight in metal. The largest, a 10-daler plate, weighed nearly 20 kg; payments had to be hauled by cart.

lead.en: The Thirty Years' War ends and state sovereignty is born

summary.en: Treaties signed at Münster and Osnabrück ended the devastating Thirty Years' War. Dutch and Swiss independence was recognised, and the principle of state sovereignty became the basis of the European international order.

lead.en: Cossacks sail between Asia and America 80 years before Bering

summary.en: In 1648 an expedition led by the Cossack Semyon Dezhnev and Fedot Popov rounded the north-eastern tip of Asia, sailing through the strait between Asia and America eighty years before Vitus Bering.

title.en: Execution of Charles I of England

lead.en: Parliament tries its king and England becomes a republic

summary.en: Defeated in civil war against Parliament, King Charles I was tried for treason and beheaded outside Whitehall Palace. England became a republic, soon dominated by Oliver Cromwell.

lead.en: A ships' supply post grows into the seed of Cape Town

summary.en: Jan van Riebeeck set up a Dutch East India Company station at Table Bay to supply ships bound for Asia. The settlement at the Cape of Good Hope grew into Cape Town and the starting point of colonisation in South Africa.

lead.en: Dutch sailors spend 13 years trapped in Korea

summary.en: In 1653 a Dutch ship was wrecked off Jeju. Korea let no foreigners leave, so the survivors lived there for 13 years until Hamel and others escaped by boat to Japan. His journal became the first European account of Korea — written partly to claim back pay for those years.

lead.en: Khmelnytsky swears to the tsar; Left-bank Ukraine joins Moscow

summary.en: In January 1654 Hetman Bohdan Khmelnytsky and the Zaporozhian Cossacks swore allegiance to Tsar Alexis. Moscow's acquisition of Cossack Ukraine led to the Russo-Polish War of 1654–1667.

lead.en: Humans wipe out Mauritius's flightless bird in under a century

summary.en: In 1662 sailors from the wrecked Dutch ship Arnhem described dodos on an islet off Mauritius, the last widely accepted sighting. Hunting and introduced animals wiped the bird out within a century of discovery. Meanwhile, Louis XIV was beginning to rebuild Versailles.

lead.en: A messianic fever grips the Jewish world, then collapses

summary.en: In 1665 the prophet Nathan of Gaza proclaimed the Smyrna kabbalist Sabbatai Zevi the Messiah, and within months the news swept communities from Yemen to Amsterdam; people sold their property to prepare for the return to the Holy Land. In 1666 the Ottoman authorities arrested Sabbatai, and under threat of death he converted to Islam. The collapse shook the Jewish world, though his secret followers, the Dönme, survived in Turkey into the 20th century.

lead.en: Nikon's reforms give birth to the Old Believers

summary.en: The Great Moscow Synod of 1666–1667 upheld Patriarch Nikon's church reforms and anathematised those who kept the old rite. This gave rise to the Old Believers; their leader Archpriest Avvakum was exiled and later burned.

title.en: Treaty of Breda: nutmeg for Manhattan

lead.en: The Dutch keep a nutmeg islet; the English keep New York

summary.en: The Second Anglo-Dutch War ended on the basis of "keep what you hold". The Dutch kept the tiny island of Run in Indonesia, a source of precious nutmeg, while England kept New Amsterdam, captured in 1664 and already renamed New York.

lead.en: A Cossack revolt sweeps the Volga from Astrakhan to Simbirsk

summary.en: In 1670 the Don Cossack Stenka Razin raised a revolt along the Volga, taking Tsaritsyn, Astrakhan and Saratov. His army was defeated at Simbirsk; in 1671 Razin was handed over and executed in Moscow.

lead.en: Shivaji crowns himself and founds the Maratha state

summary.en: The Maratha leader Shivaji, who had fought the Mughals for years, was crowned Chhatrapati at the fortress of Raigad. The Maratha state he founded became the leading power in India in the 18th century.

lead.en: A drop of water reveals an invisible living world

summary.en: Cloth merchant Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground his own lenses and in 1676 wrote to the Royal Society about "animalcules" in a drop of water. It was the first time anyone had seen bacteria and protists.

lead.en: A ten-year-old takes the throne — Russia's future reformer

summary.en: In 1682 ten-year-old Peter was proclaimed tsar; after the Streltsy uprising he shared the throne with his half-brother Ivan V under the regency of Sophia. Peter ruled alone from 1696 and launched sweeping reforms.

lead.en: Sobieski lifts the siege and the Ottoman retreat begins

summary.en: An army led by Polish king John III Sobieski lifted the Ottoman siege of Vienna, routing Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa. The defeat began the Ottoman Empire's retreat from Central Europe.

lead.en: A London coffee house grows into a global insurance market

summary.en: Around 1686 Edward Lloyd opened a coffee house frequented by sailors, merchants and shipowners. He published shipping news, cargoes were insured at its tables, and so began Lloyd’s, the world’s great insurance market.

lead.en: Laws of motion and gravity lay the base of classical physics

summary.en: Isaac Newton published the Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, setting out his three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation. One mechanics for heaven and Earth became the foundation of classical physics.

lead.en: A nearly bloodless coup makes Parliament supreme

summary.en: Parliament invited the Dutch stadtholder William of Orange, and the Catholic James II fled almost without a fight. The Bill of Rights curbed royal power and established the supremacy of Parliament, the basis of Britain's constitutional monarchy.

lead.en: Russia and Qing China agree their first border

summary.en: Russia's first treaty with Qing China, negotiated by Fyodor Golovin, fixed the border along the Argun River and mountain ranges. Russia gave up the Amur basin but gained peace and trade with China for a century and a half.

title.en: The pirate haven of Île Sainte-Marie

lead.en: A pirate supply depot off Madagascar, stocked from New York

summary.en: Around 1691 the fugitive Englishman Adam Baldridge set up a trading post for Indian Ocean pirates on an island off Madagascar. He sold them rum, powder and food shipped by the New York merchant Frederick Philipse, and sent the loot back. Henry Every, Thomas Tew and William Kidd all called here.

lead.en: Not a single 'witch' was burned at Salem

summary.en: In 1692–93 more than 200 people in colonial Massachusetts were accused of witchcraft. Twenty were executed and none was burned: nineteen were hanged and one man was pressed to death with stones for refusing to plead.

lead.en: The first great gold rush of the modern era

summary.en: In the 1690s bandeirantes, slave-hunters and treasure-seekers from São Paulo, found gold in Brazil's interior. Hundreds of thousands of Portuguese poured into the region named Minas Gerais ('General Mines'), along with masses of enslaved Africans. Brazilian gold filled Lisbon's treasury and built Baroque towns such as Ouro Preto, and in 1763 the colonial capital moved to Rio de Janeiro.

lead.en: The richest pirate raid and the first worldwide manhunt

summary.en: In September 1695 the English pirate Henry Every captured a ship of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb returning from Mecca. The haul was so vast that the East India Company and the English crown launched history's first worldwide manhunt. Every was never caught.

title.en: Fall of Nojpetén, the last Maya kingdom

lead.en: The Itza held out almost 180 years after the Aztecs fell

place.en: Flores island, Lake Petén Itzá, Guatemala

summary.en: Nojpetén, capital of the Itza Maya, stood on an island in a lake deep in the Petén jungle, long out of Spanish reach. Only on 13 March 1697 did Martín de Ursúa's force, using a galley built on the shore, storm the city. So fell the last independent Maya kingdom, almost two centuries after first contact with Europeans. The town of Flores stands on the site today.

lead.en: A 2-metre tsar tours Europe incognito as a shipwright

summary.en: Peter I travelled to Europe as 'Peter Mikhailov' and from September 1697 worked as a shipwright in Dutch yards, then studied shipbuilding in England. Staying unrecognised was hopeless: at about 2.03 m he towered over everyone around him.

lead.en: Want a beard? Pay up and carry a copper beard token

summary.en: Back from Europe, Peter I taxed beards. Under a 1705 decree rich merchants paid 100 roubles a year, townsmen 60 or 30, and peasants a kopek every time they entered a town. Payers carried a token showing a beard and the words 'money taken'.

title.en: Guru Gobind Singh founds the Khalsa

lead.en: Why Sikh men are named Singh and wear the turban

summary.en: At the Vaisakhi festival of 1699 the tenth Sikh Guru, Gobind Singh, called for volunteers ready to die for their faith; thus came the 'five beloved ones', the first members of the Khalsa. The initiated vowed to wear five articles of faith, including uncut hair and a dagger, and took the names Singh ('lion') and Kaur ('princess').
